problem: "leaked paper images" is ambiguous; a student cannot tell whether it means exam papers, newspapers or printed photos.
fix: "... newsroom verification and photographs of a leaked question paper."

problem: The heading says "three kinds of mark", but the third item, steganography, hides the existence of a message rather than embedding a mark; the list mixing a mark, a technique and a per-copy mark confuses the vocabulary.
fix: Retitle it "Four goals and three hiding techniques", and say the steganographic payload is the hidden message, while a watermark or a fingerprint is the embedded mark.

problem: "Watermark: ownership proof or tamper check" is stated but never explained; the chapter never says why some watermarks reveal editing and others survive editing.
fix: Add one line: a fragile watermark is designed to break on any edit, so its absence or damage signals tampering; a robust watermark is designed to survive compression, cropping and scaling, so it can prove ownership.

problem: The model answer says a mid-frequency DCT mark "is changed in the same transform domain", which does not by itself explain survival and can be copied by a student as a non-answer.
fix: Say: JPEG throws away information mainly in the fine pixel detail, so LSB bits become effectively random after quantisation; a mark placed in mid-frequency DCT coefficients with enough strength stays detectable because ordinary quality factors change those coefficients only moderately, and the detector correlates over many blocks.

problem: The closing sentence claims "the same evidence pipeline appears in 6.8", but the clause that follows describes camera output volume, not the read-metadata / detect-copy-move / hash-and-custody pipeline; the cross-reference asserts content of another chapter that may not match.
fix: Check what 6.8 actually covers and either link to its real topic (for example, surveillance video volume) or drop the sentence. If kept, write it as: "6.8 looks at the other end of the same problem: cameras produce media faster than people can watch it, which is why automated forensic checks are needed."
